articles.body: Working with a report on one side and source material on the other is a common setup. Getting there by dragging window edges with the mouse rarely lines up exactly, and you redo it each time a window gets moved. TL;DR: Win+Left or Win+Right snaps a window to half the screen; Win+Up and Win+Down resize it. The shortcuts Win+Left / Win+Right snaps the active window to the left or right half of the screen. Report on the left, reference on the right. Win+Up makes the window bigger. On a window that's snapped to one half, the first press moves it to the top quarter of the screen; press it again to fill the screen. Win+Down restores a maximized window to its previous size. All of these were pressed and checked on Windows 11.

articles.title: Your AI quoted $1,850. Your salesperson quoted $2,400. The customer saw both.
articles.excerpt: A commercial cleaning company asked me to look at their AI receptionist because "it keeps giving the wrong prices." I pulled 143 quotes from one quarter — every enquiry where the AI had produced a num…
articles.body: A commercial cleaning company asked me to look at their AI receptionist because "it keeps giving the wrong prices." I pulled 143 quotes from one quarter — every enquiry where the AI had produced a number and a human had later quoted the same job. 59 of them disagreed. That's 41%. The average gap was 18%, and in one case the AI said $1,850 and the account manager quoted $2,400 for the same square footage and the same frequency. The customer had both numbers in writing, four days apart. It was never a model problem My first assumption was hallucination. It wasn't. I read the transcripts. The AI was reading from a real document — a 2023 price sheet in a shared drive. The salesperson was reading from a 2025 sheet in his own email. The CRM had a third set of numbers that matched neither.
articles.author: chenwengui23

articles.title: Designing approvals
articles.excerpt: Not every action deserves the same approval. A read-only lookup risks nothing. A routine update risks a little. A consequential action risks a lot. Most approval flows ignore that. They follow the org…
articles.body: Not every action deserves the same approval. A read-only lookup risks nothing. A routine update risks a little. A consequential action risks a lot. Most approval flows ignore that. They follow the org chart instead of the risk. Everything waits for the same manager. Everything takes the same two days. The low-risk work stalls, and the high-risk work gets the same rubber stamp as everything else. Practitioners wrote the real rules for us, and none of them are in any API contract. Testimonials need a human before they go live. Escalation happens after two contacts. Refunds under fifty dollars are fine when the order is paid and never refunded before. Timeline rules nobody wrote down anywhere. Those are not edge cases. Those are the approval flow.
articles.author: HIVE

articles.title: Claude Code Agent Loop Deep Dive (7): Retries and Eight Layers of Error Recovery
articles.excerpt: Earlier posts covered semantic recovery inside the agent loop: raising the output-token limit, compacting an overlong context, and handling stop reasons. A production agent also encounters infrastruct…
articles.body: Earlier posts covered semantic recovery inside the agent loop: raising the output-token limit, compacting an overlong context, and handling stop reasons. A production agent also encounters infrastructure failures: The network fails before a request reaches the API. The API returns a 500 server error. A 429 rate limit is reached. A 529 reports an overloaded Anthropic cluster. The API rejects the request as prompt_too_long . Claude Code does not handle those cases with one generic retry. It layers retries, server-directed backoff, model fallback, context recovery, and hard stop conditions so that a single user request has the best possible chance of finishing without manual intervention. Every API call goes through withRetry Claude Code never makes a bare model request.
articles.author: Zhengxin

articles.title: Uptime Monitoring: Test the Application, Not Only the Server
articles.excerpt: A server can respond to a network probe while the website fails to serve its users. Useful monitoring measures the service people actually depend on. An HTTP check can confirm that a page responds wit…
articles.body: A server can respond to a network probe while the website fails to serve its users. Useful monitoring measures the service people actually depend on. Choose a meaningful check An HTTP check can confirm that a page responds with an expected status and a small piece of expected content. A generic success page from a reverse proxy is not proof that the application behind it is working. For a database dependent application, consider a restricted health endpoint designed to reveal only necessary status. Avoid exposing credentials, environment variables, internal addresses, or detailed errors. Separate availability from performance Record response time as well as success. A site that responds too slowly can still harm the user experience even if the monitor calls it available.
articles.author: Alif Host

articles.title: Checkout Failure Reconstruction: Node.js SaaS Alerting API, Poll Queries, and Webhooks
articles.excerpt: Short answer: use a queryable error alerting API with a durable cursor for Node.js SaaS checkout failures, then choose polling or a webhook based on detection latency; use a separate heartbeat for a c…
articles.body: Short answer: use a queryable error alerting API with a durable cursor for Node.js SaaS checkout failures, then choose polling or a webhook based on detection latency; use a separate heartbeat for a checkout that never emits an error event. For a media SaaS checkout, the useful design is a small event pipeline with durable context and a separate delivery worker. The decision is driven by incident reconstruction: the alert must tell the on-call engineer which checkout failed, at what stage, and what the customer saw, instead of only saying that an exception occurred. That sounds obvious until a payment authorization times out after a subscription is created. A single stack trace may be accurate and still be a poor incident record.
articles.author: EchoF76

articles.title: HTTPS Troubleshooting: Certificate Problems and Mixed Content Are Different
articles.excerpt: A browser warning after enabling HTTPS can come from several layers. Replacing a certificate will not fix every problem, and changing application URLs will not repair an expired certificate. Confirm t…
articles.body: A browser warning after enabling HTTPS can come from several layers. Replacing a certificate will not fix every problem, and changing application URLs will not repair an expired certificate. Check the hostname Confirm the exact address visitors use. A certificate covering the root domain does not necessarily cover every subdomain. Check the certificate names, validity period, and chain presented by the public endpoint. If a CDN or reverse proxy is involved, distinguish the connection from visitor to proxy from the connection between proxy and origin. Both need a configuration appropriate to the deployment. Look for mixed content A page can load over HTTPS while requesting images, scripts, or styles over HTTP.

An orbital view reveals the immense beauty of our blue planet, the only world we know of that hosts life. But it also highlights how fragile that life is, tethered to our lonely Earth in the vast void of space, according to Crew-12 commander Jessica Meir of NASA. "You see this very thin, tenuous band of an atmosphere , and you know that that is all that is supporting life, and we really need to do our best to protect it," Meir said on Thursday afternoon (Oct. 15), during a press conference that discussed the recently concluded Crew-12 mission .

articles.body: Using data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers have unraveled some of the atmospheric secrets of a bizarre, blisteringly hot world that has the consistency of marshmallow. The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet , under the watchful infrared eye of the JWST , is WASP-17b, located around 1,300 light-years away. The exoplanet has a mass around 0.8 times that of Jupiter, but it is around twice as wide as the solar system's largest planet, giving it a "super-puff" consistency comparable to the Earth-based treat. WASP-17 b is so close to its parent star that it completes an orbit in under four Earth days, with this proximity also making the temperature of this " hot Jupiter " skyrocket.

articles.title: How to see the Orionid meteor shower 2026 peak this week — and when to look
articles.excerpt: The Orionids peak around Oct. 21. Here's when and where to look for the best chance of spotting meteors.
articles.body: If you love watching meteors, 2026 has given you plenty to enjoy. This summer, the annual Perseid meteor shower peaked on the day of a new moon — and a solar eclipse — so moonlight stayed out of the way. And there's more to look forward to: in December, the Geminids, the year's most prolific shower, will peak after a waxing crescent moon sets early in the evening, opening the door to excellent viewing. Right between those two headline showers, the dependable Orionids take their turn, reaching peak activity around Oct. 21-22. So, when and where can you catch the show? When and where to watch Make sure you wrap up warm for a night of Orionid hunting.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 16, 1975: NASA launches the 1st-ever GOES weather satellite to watch Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 16, 1975, NASA launched the first operational GOES weather satellite. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 16, 1975, NASA launched the first operational GOES satellite! GOES-A was the first in a series of weather satellites that NASA jointly operated with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). The name is short for Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite . GOES-A launched on a Delta rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida. GOES satellites all have a geostationary orbit, which means they always face the same part of Earth — in this case, the Indian Ocean. Once GOES-A became operational, it was renamed GOES-1. The GOES satellite fleet has grown over the years, and is a critical link in the chain of satellites tracking Earth's weather from space.
